fields.expected: I would want to work on infrastructure for scientific research and evaluation, most likely at an early-stage company or one of the newer research organizations. Over the past year I've independently studied how research gets funded and selected, reading through the history from patronage to the German research university to Bell Labs to the postwar NIH/NSF project-grant model, and then talking with researchers, research administrators, economists, and people building alternative institutions. I started out thinking the main constraint was grant-writing time and compensation. Conversations changed that: I now think the bigger effect is selection, since researchers learn which ideas are legible enough to survive review and may never attempt the ones that are hard to justify in advance. What interests me now is that AI is making generation cheap while judgment stays scarce, so I'd want to build systems for methodological validation, provenance, uncertainty, evidence tracing, and escalation to domain experts. The adjacent version of this is talent: I built tSearch, which expands through public GitHub and Substack collaboration graphs and runs rubric-driven LLM judges that return "insufficient evidence" rather than a low score when public work is missing. Both are the same problem of surfacing work conventional systems fail to evaluate well.

fields.expected: The hardest problem I've worked on was estimating sleep without a wearable for ClarityAtlas, the iOS health product I lead technically. The premise was that most people who would benefit from understanding their sleep don't own a watch, so I only had phone signals: HealthKit step counts, gait speed, and Core Motion movement patterns, plus phone-interaction timing. None of those directly observe sleep. The absence of data can mean someone is asleep, or that the phone is on a desk, or that they left it at home, and treating all three the same produced obviously wrong sessions. I ended up building a passive estimation system that combined motion and interaction signals rather than trusting any single channel, and testing it against how users actually described their own nights. The second hard part was Sleep Twins, a backend service that matches users on behavioral similarity. Raw features are on wildly different scales, so I standardized them and used a weighted distance so that the dimensions we cared about actually drove matches instead of whichever feature had the largest variance. What I took from it was that in health products the modeling failure modes users notice are almost always about ambiguous or missing data, not accuracy on clean cases. We shipped it into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users.

fields.expected: During Hopkins' Lighting of the Quads, my cofounders and I realized President Ron Daniels was somewhere nearby. We tracked him to Garland Hall, could see him through the locked doors, and knocked until someone let us in so we could pitch Open Health Intelligence on the spot. That conversation turned into a formal meeting months later with him and leadership from the Data Science and AI Institute. I'm proud of it less because of the meeting and more because it corrected something in how I thought about building. I had assumed that if the product was good enough, the right people would eventually find it. They don't. Recruiting users, explaining repeatedly why something should exist, and getting institutional support turned out to matter as much as the code, and none of that happens unless you're willing to be slightly inappropriate about asking. I now default to asking directly rather than waiting for a process to surface me, which is also how I ended up working with people well outside Hopkins on my own projects.

fields.expected: Forward Deployed Software Engineer resonates more with what I've actually enjoyed doing. At Intelehealth I worked on AI and data systems for rural telemedicine, and the work only made sense once I understood the setting. I built a resource-availability scoring pipeline in Python across 32 villages that combined facility-tier classification, geospatial distance, Google Maps data, weather, and healthcare-resource availability, because a care recommendation that ignores whether a clinic is reachable during monsoon season isn't useful. I also designed an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard using stratified sampling, which taught me that generating an answer is cheap and deciding whether it should be trusted is the hard part. I see the same thing in the anomaly-detection system I work on at Summer Atlantic Capital, where I built the temporal sequence models and a learning-to-rank layer for alerts, plus a retrieval-augmented explanation layer. An anomaly system that fires too often just creates a second problem for the analyst, so prioritization and explanation quality are the real product. That pattern of sitting close to the people using the system, learning their constraints, and then building infrastructure that generalizes is the part I would want to work on.
